newsitem.title: KENYA: Four Rwandan genocide suspects flown to Tanzania.
newsitem.headline: Four Rwandan genocide suspects flown to Tanzania.

text.p: Four Rwandans indicted for genocide by a United Nations criminal tribunal on the mass slaughter arrived at its Tanzania headquarters from Cameroon on Thursday, a tribunal spokesman said.
They included Theoneste Bagosora, the former cabinet director in Rwanda's defence ministry, accused of directing events in the first days of the 1994 genocide of an estimated 800,000 people.
He was arrested in Cameroon in March last year and was widely considered one of Rwanda's most wanted men accused of genocide.
"The four accused have arrived at the tribunal's headquarters ...They are now in detention," said tribunal spokesman Bocar Sy by telephone from the northern Tanzanian farming town of Arusha.
Cameroon President Paul Biya delayed the transfer of the four men leading to protracted negotiations with the tribunal.

"The transfer marks a capital turning point for the credibility of the international tribunal and demonstrates the tribunal's capability to prosecute the principal perpetrators of the 1994 genocide in Rwanda," Chief Prosecutor Louise Arbour said in a statement.

The other three are Anatole Nsengiyumva, a former lieutenant -colonel, Andre Ntagerura, a former minister of transport, and Ferdinand Nahimana, a senior representative of extremist Radio Mille Collines.
A total of 21 people have been indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR). The arrival of the four took to 11 the number of suspects in detention at its headquarters.
The tribunal was set up in November 1994 to bring to justice the main architects of the three-month genocide in Rwanda of Tutsis and Hutu moderates by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs.

Earlier on Thursday, the tribunal's first trial heard from a prosecution witness how a former Hutu mayor accused of genocide and crimes against humanity hounded a Tutsi political enemy he wanted killed.
The witness said accused Jean-Paul Akayesu, 43, told a public meeting in central Taba commune that Ephraim Karangwa should be hunted down as he collaborated with the rebel Rwanda Patriotic Front.
Akayesu has pleaded not guilty. If convicted he faces life imprisonment, the tribunal's highest penalty.
The witness told how Akayesu invented a feud with Karangwa to justify his death.

"I have a list of people here who should be killed and the first one is Ephraim Karangwa because he wants to kill me and take over the mayorship," the witness, known as "V" in a bid to protect his identity, quoted Akayesu as telling the meeting.
Karangwa survived the 1994 genocide and is due to testify before the tribunal, according to the prosecution's indictment.
The prosecution rates the feud between Akayesu and Karangwa as a key element in massacres in Taba commune.
Witness "V" is the 11th in the two-week-old trial and gave evidence to lead prosecutor Yacob Haile-Mariam of Ethiopia.
Presiding judge Laity Kama of Senegal adjourned the trial until Friday.
